Giugiaro's Peralta D Is the Hand-Made Copper-Body Gran Tourer, No One's Rich Enough To Have Another
22 photos
Photo: GFG Style
You’d never thought that, in this speed-crazed, high-tech-junkie society of ours, automotive design would take a step toward the very beginnings of man. And yet, the bold Italians behind the Peralta D one-off have done just that – catapulted the personal transportation paradigm straight to the copper age, when homo Sapiens were just learning to fabricate tools out of pure copper. This is what GFG Style proposes some ten millennia later – a car made out of copper.
Throughout the history of automotive engineering, carmakers have relied on a familiar roster of materials to shape their vehicles’ bodies. Steel has long served as the traditional industrial workhorse, while lightweight aluminum, crafted wood, molded fiberglass, exotic carbon fiber, and various specialized alloys have all taken turns defining the silhouettes of modern transportation.
Yet, one question has rarely crossed the minds of automotive designers: when did a manufacturer ever think of sculpting an entire car shell out of pure copper?
Well, that moment has arrived right now, because GFG Style just made it happen. While copper is typically reserved for electrical wiring, plumbing, or heavy industrial applications, its employment in outer automotive shells has been virtually non-existent. Although this noble, malleable metal has been known to mankind since the dawn of civilization, it took a daring bespoke project to finally hammer it into a functional, rolling sculpture for the road.
(Take “hammering” literally, please, as we can see in the embedded video at the bottom of this story. Soft metals have traditionally been shaped with wooden mallets, which are gentle enough with the material to not destroy it upon impact, but strong enough to ply it according to the craftsman’s plans).
Photo: GFG Style Outside of heavy industry, copper has always found its most celebrated traditional uses in heirloom kitchenware and moonshine stills. For centuries, giant simmering cauldrons, heavy preserving pans, and intricate distillation alembics have been shaped by master artisans relying on just two basic assets: a simple set of hand tools and an immense reservoir of metal-working skills.
Taking that exact same ancestral craft of beating raw sheets over anvils and applying it to a modern supercar chassis is a bold leap across centuries of metallurgy. One that pays homage not just to manufacturing greatness, but to the very essence of our species’ evolution astray from the rest of the animal kingdom.
The organization behind this achievement is GFG Style, an advanced styling consultancy established in 2015 in Moncalieri, near Turin, Italy, by the legendary father-and-son duo Giorgetto and Fabrizio Giugiaro. Giorgetto is celebrated the world over as one of the most prolific automotive designers in history, while Fabrizio brings over 30 years of expertise in car design and architecture.
Photo: GFG Style Together, the pair have developed over 200 prototypes and more than 300 production models for numerous global manufacturers. Not a single one of their creations has gone unnoticed, or has ever been lost in the vast sea of automotive happenings (or mishaps, but the Giugiaros have never been known for making “alright” designs).
Their latest creation stems from a close friendship and creative collaboration with Mexican entrepreneur and car collector Carlos Peralta. Following the enthusiastic reception of their previous joint project, the one-off Peralta S, the collector commissioned a second bespoke vehicle.
Officially unveiled on October 24 at the prestigious 2026 Pastejé Automotive Invitational in Mexico, the new supercar is christened the Peralta D. While the previous model honored the commissioner's sons, the letter “D” celebrates his daughters and the Italian word "donne," meaning women.
Photo: GFG Style Personally overseen at every stage by Fabrizio Giugiaro, the Peralta D is a striking 2+2 Gran Turismo coupe defined by a monolithic form and minimalist geometric harmony. When viewed from above, the sleek, uninterrupted surfaces appear continuous, as if drawn with a single pencil stroke.
A pronounced waistline divides the exterior into two distinct zones: a lower body hammered entirely by hand from pure copper, and an upper canopy crafted from mirrored glass treated to replicate the warm hue of the metal.
Beneath this artisanal copper skin lies a modern structural architecture. The hand-beaten body panels are supported by a rigid carbon-fiber structure mounted onto a lightweight aluminum chassis (I told you so). To maintain pure visual elegance, all exterior carbon-fiber elements, including the integrated front blade spoiler and rear tailpipes, are deliberately concealed from plain sight.
The coupe rides on anthracite black wheels featuring a retro-futuristic geometric pattern inspired by the 1970s that enhances the visual impact of the bodywork.
Photo: GFG Style The vehicle derives its mechanical platform and energy source from the modern Maserati GranTurismo. While the Turin design house has kept exact exterior dimensions, curb weight, and specific engine output figures closely guarded for this private commission, utilizing top-of-the-line Maserati mechanical components is bound to deliver genuine supercar performance and grand touring dynamics.
Even the fuel cap is integrated into the geometric harmony of the copper panels, confirming an internal combustion engine beneath the sculpted metal. Which makes perfect sense, since fire and copper have been humanity’s long-standing pillars of evolution ever since we decided to make tools.
Both the front and rear fascias are punctuated by sharp blades of light and geometric diamond-shaped grilles crafted from solid-machined, laser-cut aluminum. These grilles integrate and conceal the functional lamps to create a dramatic "shadow lights" effect. Noticeably absent from the flanks are traditional side doors.
Photo: GFG Style Instead, cabin ingress is achieved through a sophisticated forward-lifting dome that maintains independent side windows, evolving the single-motion canopy concept introduced on the earlier Peralta S. believe it or not, Giugiaro is copying shamelessly on this one. He’s copying himself, though – his 1963 self who crafted the one-off Chevrolet Corvair Testudo, a fabulous machine with the exact same forward-tilting gadgetry.
To solve the age-old problem of cramped rear-seat entry in two-door coupes, Fabrizio Giugiaro paired the front canopy with an innovative rear gull-wing opening mechanism that requires no underlying structural pillars. This clever engineering solution provides effortless access to the back seats and pays direct homage to the historic gull-wing rear lids his father Giorgetto developed for the classic De Tomaso Mangusta back in 1967.
Inside the four-seat cabin, the monolithic exterior theme continues through ergonomic seats upholstered in metallic-effect leather that echoes the warm copper tones outside. The hides on the seats, dashboard, and door panels are complemented by perforated Alcantara inserts and stitched together using genuine copper thread.
Photo: GFG Style The symmetrical dashboard features a digital instrument cluster on the left for the driver, balanced on the right by a dedicated passenger makeup station complete with cosmetic compartments and a monitor that doubles as an illuminated mirror.
Tucked neatly into the rear section of the center console is a final bespoke luxury touch: a retractable refrigerator engineered to hold a bottle of champagne alongside four custom drinking glasses crafted, naturally, from pure copper. I told you mankind has been very fond of copper for several reasons – and one of those revolves around turning fruits and vegetables into liquid joy. The Italians have just created one more reason for us to worship element 29 in chemistry’s periodic table.
